elicitation_input.question: Can I leave a job at the end of a trial period?
elicitation_input.question_type: Directed question that has a single unambiguous answer

llm_generation.text:
Yes. In most places, you can leave a job at the end of a trial or probationary period—and usually you can resign during it as well.

Key points:

- **Check your contract or offer letter.** It may specify a shorter notice period during probation, often about **1 week**, **2 weeks**, or **1 month**. Some contracts require the same notice period throughout employment.
- **If there is no written notice clause**, the legal default depends on your country/state. In many jurisdictions, employment is effectively **at-will**, meaning either side can end employment without notice, subject to limited exceptions.
- **Give written notice.** A short email or letter is usually enough: state that you are resigning, give the date, and identify your intended final working day.
- **You do not need to wait until the final day of probation.** If the role is not right for you, you can usually resign earlier, subject to your notice obligations.
- **Your employer may end employment sooner.** In some contracts, the employer can choose to pay you instead of having you work your notice period, often called “payment in lieu of notice.”
- **Check practical issues:** final pay, unused holiday/PTO, return of equipment, confidentiality obligations, non-compete/non-solicitation clauses, bonus or training-repayment terms, and visa sponsorship if applicable.

A simple resignation message could be:

> Dear [Manager],  
> Please accept this email as notice of my resignation from my role as [Job Title]. Under my contract, my notice period is [X], so my last working day will be [date]. Thank you for the opportunity.  
> Kind regards,  
> [Name]

If you tell me your country and what your contract says about probation and notice, I can explain the likely rules more specifically.
